records.name: Tenis
records.facts_used: The Siliņš dictionary refers Tenis to Antons. It separately mentions a mythological Tenis, a guardian of pigs. The catalogue does not establish which of these routes explains the personal name, so neither is presented here as its certain origin. The Siliņš catalogue records a historical detail: Koknese, 1599; calendar 1817 (dictionary page 304). This dates an attributed record of use and calendar inclusion. It does not mean that the name was created then, and the dates for Antons are not transferred to Tenis.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Siliņš catalogue (cached LV-SILINS-TENIS-R83), dictionary p. 304. Both the Antons cross-reference and the mythological pig-guardian Tenis are reported without choosing either; Antons’ 1752/1767 dates were not transferred. Rajandi’s note that St Anthony was invoked against pig diseases (EE-RAJANDI66 PDF 26) was deliberately not used to bridge the two routes: that would be an unverified inference.

records.name: Denise
records.facts_used: The catalogue treats Denise as the feminine form of Dionīss, a name family connected with Greek Dionysios. Behind the Name likewise describes Denise as the French feminine form of Denis. The link is to the name family, not a meaning predicted for each bearer. The Siliņš catalogue gives calendar inclusion in 1915 and a recorded use in 1929 (dictionary pages 97; 99). These date the calendar entry and an attributed use. They do not mean that the name was created then, and they are not transferred to the related Latvian spellings Denīza or Denīze.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Siliņš catalogue (cached LV-SILINS-DENISE-R83), pp. 97; 99: calendar 1915, record 1929. INT-BTN Denise cached as INT-BTN-DENISE. Dates are not transferred to Denīza/Denīze.

records.name: Denīza
records.facts_used: The Latvian name-rendering manual gives the exact English correspondence Denise → Denīza. The Language Agency database also renders Portuguese Denisa as Denīza. Denise is a French feminine form of Denis in the Dionysios family; the documented rows show how the spelling is adapted, not every bearer’s naming route. The English row appears in the 2006 manual on printed page 98; the Portuguese recommendation is dated 2015 (page 134). These date published rendering recommendations. They do not identify the first Latvian birth registration, and the older calendar dates of Denise are not transferred to Denīza.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Visually checked LV-LVA-EN06 PDF p. 95 / printed p. 98: Denise [də´ni:z] → Denīza. Portuguese Denisa → Denīza (Placinska 2015 p. 134) read in the Language Agency search result only (cached WEB-PERSONVARDUATVEIDE-…-Q-DEN-C4-ABZA); that PDF page was not inspected. No Latvian first-use date.

records.name: Denīze
records.facts_used: The Language Agency database gives the exact French correspondence Denise → Denīze, citing Ceplītis’s 1963 guidance (page 76), and the same Latvian form for Portuguese Denise (2015). Denise is the French feminine form of Denis, in the family of Greek Dionysios. Laimute Balode and Renāte Siliņa-Piņķe (2025, printed page 148) list Denīze among the top 200 newborn names registered in Latvia in 2018–2022, as an international name adapted to Latvian spelling. This dates recent popularity, not the name’s first Latvian use.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: French Denise → Denīze (Ceplītis 1963 p. 76) and Portuguese Denise → Denīze (Placinska 2015 p. 134) read in the Language Agency search result (cached WEB-PERSONVARDUATVEIDE-…-Q-DEN-C4-ABZE); the 1963 printed page was not independently inspected. LV-IDENTITY25 PDF p. 11 / printed p. 148 visually checked: Denīze among top-200 newborn names 2018–2022. records.name: Dionisijs
records.facts_used: The catalogue refers Dionisijs to Dionizijs and that form to Dioniss, a form of the Greek personal name Dionysios. In Greek mythology Dionysos is the god of ecstasy and wine. The chain links the spellings; it does not give Dionisijs a separate meaning. The Siliņš catalogue records a historical detail: Rīga, 1366 (dictionary page 99). The same year is attached to the linked Dionizijs entry, so it keeps that shared scope. It dates an attributed record of use, not the creation of this modern spelling.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Siliņš catalogue (cached LV-SILINS-DIONISIJS-R83), p. 99. The 1366 Rīga date is shared with Dionizijs; the catalogue states the chain does not give a separate meaning.

records.name: Dioniss
records.facts_used: The catalogue explains Dioniss as a form of the Greek personal name Dionysios; in Greek mythology Dionysos is the god of ecstasy and wine. Behind the Name notes that the Latin form Dionysius was borne by Dionysius the Areopagite in the New Testament and by many early saints. The Siliņš catalogue records a historical detail: Rīga, first quarter of the twentieth century (dictionary page 99). This dates an attributed record of use. It does not mean that the name was created then, and the 1366 date of the linked Dionizijs entry is not transferred to Dioniss.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Siliņš catalogue (cached LV-SILINS-DIONISS-R83), p. 99. INT-BTN Dionysius cached as INT-BTN-DIONYSIUS. 1366 not transferred.

records.name: Dionizijs

records.name: Radions
records.facts_used: The Ukrainian name-rendering manual gives the exact correspondence Радіон → Radions, beside Родіон → Rodions. The Siliņš dictionary also refers Radions to Rodions, which it compares with Greek Rhodion, “inhabitant of the island of Rhodes”; its alternative link with rhodon, “rose”, is question-marked. The Siliņš catalogue records a historical detail: Umurga, 1906 (dictionary page 265); no calendar year is given. The manual row is dated 2023 (printed page 152). Neither date is a creation date, and the Rodions dates are not transferred to Radions.

records.name: Trofims
records.facts_used: The catalogue connects Trofims with Greek Trophimos and records several explanations: “nourisher”, as well as “nourished, brought up”. Behind the Name derives Trophimos from trophe, “nourishment”, and notes a companion of Paul of this name in the New Testament. The 1993 manual gives Russian Трофим → Trofims. The Siliņš catalogue records a historical detail: Abrene, first quarter of the twentieth century; calendar 1851 (dictionary page 309). The rendering row is on printed page 211 of the 1993 manual. These date use, calendar inclusion and a recommendation, not the name’s creation.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Siliņš catalogue (cached LV-SILINS-TROFIMS-R83), p. 309; the origin sentence on the Trofims page is worded for “Trofima”, so the Trophimos explanation may belong to a shared Trofims/Trofima entry; only the dates shown for Trofims were used. Visually checked LV-LVA-RU93 PDF p. 104 / printed p. 211 (Трофим → Trofims). INT-BTN Trophimus cached as INT-BTN-TROPHIMUS.

records.name: Beatričė
records.facts_used: The Senn–Salys dictionary pairs Beatričė with Beatrice. Behind the Name describes Beatrice as the Italian form of Beatrix; its best-known bearer is Beatrice Portinari (1266–1290), loved by the poet Dante Alighieri. That literary history belongs to the Italian name, not to any Lithuanian bearer. Salys’s Lithuanian calendar for 1964, reprinted in 1983, prints Beatričė (Beata) on 18 August. This documents the exact name and a short form in a modern calendar; that older date does not replace the name’s date in the present calendar.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Visually checked LT-SALYS83 PDF p. 218 / printed p. 203 (Beatričė PN Beatrice; separate Beatrisà = Beatrix) and PDF p. 312 / printed p. 297 (18 August: Beatričė (Beata)); August heading on PDF 311. Project date 17 January differs from the 1964 calendar; the Dante episode concerns the Italian name.

records.name: Anto
records.facts_used: Edgar Rajandi lists Anto as a short form with two possible full names, Andreas and Antonius. Under Antonius he gives Anto ~ Antu among the Estonian shortenings of Anton. The exact full name of an individual Anto therefore cannot be inferred from the short form alone. Rajandi’s Raamat nimedest was published in Tallinn in 1966 (printed page 28). It records Anto in both name families; this dates the linguistic description, not the first Estonian bearer, and dates for Tõnis or Tõnu are not transferred to Anto.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Visually checked EE-RAJANDI66 PDF p. 26 / printed p. 28: “Ant, Anti, Anto → Andreas, → Antonius” and under Antonius “Anto ~ Antu”. No dated Estonian birth record of Anto established.

records.name: Antu
records.facts_used: Edgar Rajandi gives Antu, beside Anto, among the Estonian shortenings of Anton/Antonius. He describes Antonius as Greco-Roman, from a word of unclear meaning, so no single literal sense is asserted for Antu; its supplementary list also points Antu back to Antonius. The book was published in Tallinn in 1966 (printed pages 28 and 194). It documents Antu as an Estonian short form; it does not date the first Estonian bearer, and the long history of Tõnis and Tõnu is not transferred to this rare form.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Visually checked EE-RAJANDI66 PDF p. 26 / printed p. 28 (Anto ~ Antu under Antonius) and PDF p. 192 / printed p. 194 supplementary list “Antu OKS-u (< Antonius ← Neum)”. The OKS source abbreviation was not resolved with certainty (the key on PDF 239 mixes O. Kallas lists of 1911 and 1921), so no year is claimed.

records.name: Tõnis
records.facts_used: Tõnis is an Estonian form of Antonius. Julius Mägiste (1929) equates it with Antonius and cites older written spellings such as Tönis, Tönies and Denis. Edgar Rajandi notes that the medieval veneration of Saint Anthony the hermit and Anthony of Padua supported the name’s spread. Rajandi writes that Tõnis and Tõnu spread very widely in Estonia from the fifteenth century and remained among preferred names until the mid-nineteenth century (printed page 28). Evar Saar finds the form recorded as Denis frequent in South Tartumaa in the 1580s.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Visually checked EE-MAGISTE29 cached copy PDF p. 51 / printed p. 49 (Tõnis = Antonius; KA Tönis, Tönies, Tönijes, Tonies; P 218 Denis); EE-RAJANDI66 PDF 26–27 / printed 28–29 (spread from the 15th century, preferred names until the mid-19th century; saint cult and supposed ancient Tõnn); EE-SAAR16 (local copy LOCAL-ROUND20-VORU) PDF 19 / printed 20 (1580s Denis (Tõnis ~ Tennüs) very frequent elsewhere in South Tartumaa, not in Rõuge/Vastseliina). EE-KALLASMAA17 p. 3 lists Tõnis among short forms that arrived ready-made from German areas (not used in text).

records.name: Tõnn
records.facts_used: The origin of Tõnn is debated. Edgar Rajandi and Marja Kallasmaa mention it as a name regarded as ancient Estonian, possibly replaced or merged with adaptations of Antonius; Evar Saar’s table instead places Tõnn among Antonius forms via Low German Tönnies. The question remains open. Saar notes that the written form Tyn, which he identifies with Tõnn, was very frequent in South Tartumaa in the 1580s, though not in Rõuge and Vastseliina. Julius Mägiste (1929) lists Tõnn with Saaremaa examples such as Thonj and compares it with Tõnis; these are written records, not proof of either origin.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Competing views kept open: EE-RAJANDI66 PDF 27 / printed 29 “oletatud muistne eesti nimi Tõnn”; EE-KALLASMAA17 PDF p. 3, paragraph beginning “Tõenäoliselt”, “muinasnimeks peetud Tõnn Antoniuse muganditega” (explicitly a proposal); EE-SAAR16 Appendix 1 (PDF 40 / printed 41, all Tartumaa 1582–1588) row Tyn … (Tõnn, Tõnu, Tõnis) | Tönnies, Tönne | Antonius, and PDF 19 / printed 20 “Tyn (Tõnn)” frequent in South Tartumaa in the 1580s. EE-MAGISTE29 printed p. 49: Tõnn (SB 1927 131 Thomas Thonj, 133 Thoni Janusßon, Srm., Wd.); vrd. Tõnis. All visually checked.
